analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to cap fees for changes, cancellations, and checked bags at cost.
analysis.headline: Died in committee: the FAIR Fees Act, aimed at airline change and bag fees, never got a vote after being referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2016.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write rules forbidding airlines from charging fees for flight changes, cancellations, checked bags, or anything else related to a flight that exceed the actual cost of providing the service. The Transportation Department would have had to set standards for judging when a fee is reasonable and update them every three years. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, especially travelers who fly occasionally and get hit with change fees and bag fees, which can run hundreds of dollars and often exceed what the service actually costs the airline. Since fees disproportionately hit price-sensitive travelers buying cheaper tickets, the burden falls hardest on ordinary households rather than business travelers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers paying change and bag fees

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits air carriers from imposing any fee for a flight change or cancellation, checked baggage, or any other flight-related fee that is 'unreasonable or disproportional to the costs incurred by the air carrier.' [S2] [S3]

Directs the Secretary of Transportation to set standards for judging fee reasonableness, taking into account the airline's actual costs: for change fees, the net cost after rebooking, fare differences, and the electronic processing and labor costs; for bag fees, the electronic processing and labor costs of handling bags. [S3]
Requires the Transportation Department to finalize the rules within 270 days of enactment and update the standards at least every three years. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which collected billions of dollars a year in change, cancellation, and checked bag fees that in many cases exceeded the cost of the underlying service. Fares might rise slightly as carriers reprice tickets to recover the revenue, but the heaviest charges would fall only on airlines' fee income, not on travelers directly.

drawbacks.text: The bill's approach depends heavily on regulators: it relies on the Transportation Department to define 'reasonable and proportional' and enforce the standards, which airlines would have litigated heavily and which a future administration could weaken or rewrite at each mandated three-year update. [S3]

The standard is vague by design: 'any other fee imposed by an air carrier relating to a flight' [S3] could pull in seat-selection, boarding-priority, and other ancillary charges that airlines price differently by market, so an honest supporter would have to concede the rulemaking would be contentious and the resulting caps imprecise — though the same vagueness is what gives the rule its reach over new fees airlines invent.

Airlines and many economists argue fee revenue lets carriers advertise low base fares and keep flying profitable on thin margins; capping fees could raise base fares for all passengers, including those who never check a bag or change a ticket, spreading the cost of the reform to everyone rather than the users of the service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most travelers the benefit outweighs the cost: change fees of $200 on a ticket that cost $150, or bag fees far above the marginal cost of handling a bag, are charges for services that often cost the airline little, and capping them at actual cost puts the money back in passengers' pockets. The honest caveat is that some of that fee revenue could resurface in slightly higher base fares, and the rule's effectiveness depends entirely on how aggressively the Transportation Department defines and enforces the cost standard. Even so, a rule that stops airlines from charging more than a service costs is a direct, measurable gain for the people who pay the fees.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate in March 2016, read twice, and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, where it sat until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey (D-MA) introduced the FAIR Fees Act on March 9, 2016, joined by one cosponsor, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT). [S1] [S3] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day. [S5]
No further action was taken: the bill stayed in committee until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and died without a vote or a hearing. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off: they kept charging change, cancellation, and checked bag fees without any requirement that the charges bear any relationship to their actual costs, and the revenue those fees generate was never touched.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act on March 9, 2016.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining ten months of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped change, cancellation, and bag fees at roughly what the service costs the airline, directly cutting into a major fee-revenue stream. Airlines kept that revenue when the bill died, and passengers kept paying fees that can exceed the cost of the underlying service.
